Ukraine, Russia Report Emergency App Cyberattacks as Fake Alerts Warn of Nuclear Danger
Publication: Nov. 2, 2026, 5:14 AM EST / Updated Nov. 2, 2026, 7:56 AM EST. Author: Yuliya Talmazan

Both Ukraine and Russia experienced coordinated cyberattacks on their emergency alert systems Sunday night, resulting in alarming false messages about nuclear threats and radiation hazards.

Around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time, Ukraine's emergency alert application was compromised with messages warning residents of radiation hazards, chemical threats, and street combat. One message stated: "all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert" and referenced Russia's Oreshnik hypersonic missile, claiming "Oreshnik is in action."

The hacked alerts were issued in Russian, which helped residents quickly identify them as fraudulent. Ukraine's air force confirmed the "Air Alert" app had been "compromised by the enemy" and assured the public there was no actual radiation threat.

Olena Yermakova, a 32-year-old Kyiv researcher: "I started running through a checklist in my head of what to do during a nuclear threat and whether I had all the supplies at home."

Hours later, Russia's emergencies ministry reported its mobile application suffered a "massive cyberattack" with "dissemination of fake information to the public." Russian alerts warned of "nuclear warheads" launched at Russia.

The cyberattacks occurred just as a six-day humanitarian ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia ended in the Kherson region. This truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, had successfully facilitated the evacuation of approximately 800 civilians from the frontline town of Oleshky.

Melania Trump: "I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire."

Both sides have already accused each other of using the truce period strategically—Ukraine claims Russia rotated units and fortified positions, while Russia notes that Kyiv could have similarly regrouped.
